lessons.title: AI model basics
lessons.intro: This lesson in AI Fundamentals develops ai model basics. By the end, you should be able to explain the idea, apply it to a small practical task, identify a likely mistake and justify how you checked the result. The focus is on usable foundation skills and evidence of learning.
lessons.concept:
MEANING
A model learns patterns from training data and generates predictions or content.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
AI model basics is one part of ai fundamentals, rather than a substitute for the whole workflow. Connect it to the course purpose when deciding what information or preparation is needed, and to task suitability when checking what should happen next. State which decisions belong to the user, the tool and the person reviewing the work.

PRINCIPLES
AI work is a collaboration between a tool and a responsible reviewer. A model response may be useful without being reliable enough to publish. Treat source facts, generated suggestions and verified conclusions as separate things. Do not supply private learner records merely to make a demonstration feel realistic.

METHOD AND QUALITY
Compare alternatives against accuracy, relevance, privacy and the effort required to review them. A faster workflow is not an improvement if it creates unsupported claims or hides mistakes.

COMMON MISTAKE
A learner may recognise the terminology but still be unable to demonstrate the result. Avoid replacing a practical check with a statement that the work looks correct. Keep the input, expected outcome and observed outcome so that someone else can understand your conclusion.

TERMS TO CONNECT
AI model basics; Task suitability; Prompt structure; Output verification; Privacy and responsibility; AI-assisted project.

lessons.title: Node runtime
lessons.intro: This lesson in Node.js Foundations develops node runtime. By the end, you should be able to explain the idea, apply it to a small practical task, identify a likely mistake and justify how you checked the result. The focus is on usable foundation skills and evidence of learning.
lessons.concept:
MEANING
Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
Node runtime is one part of node.js foundations, rather than a substitute for the whole workflow. Connect it to the course purpose when deciding what information or preparation is needed, and to modules and packages when checking what should happen next. State which decisions belong to the user, the tool and the person reviewing the work.

PRINCIPLES
Web work separates structure, presentation, behaviour and server responsibilities. HTML expresses meaning, CSS controls presentation and JavaScript supplies interaction. Server code must enforce permissions and protect secrets even when the interface already hides an action. Test the actual user journey rather than judging only a screenshot.

METHOD AND QUALITY
Check the happy path, empty or invalid input, keyboard use and narrow screens. Display a success message only after the intended action succeeds. A prototype and a connected production service have different responsibilities.

COMMON MISTAKE
A learner may recognise the terminology but still be unable to demonstrate the result. Avoid replacing a practical check with a statement that the work looks correct. Keep the input, expected outcome and observed outcome so that someone else can understand your conclusion.

TERMS TO CONNECT
Node runtime; Modules and packages; Asynchronous work; HTTP services; Server validation; Node service project.

The focus is on usable foundation skills and evidence of learning.
lessons.concept:
MEANING
Define who the campaign serves and the business result it should support.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
Audience and objectives is one part of digital marketing foundations, rather than a substitute for the whole workflow. Connect it to the course purpose when deciding what information or preparation is needed, and to customer journey when checking what should happen next. State which decisions belong to the user, the tool and the person reviewing the work.

PRINCIPLES
A campaign needs an audience, a useful offer and a business objective. Content, distribution and measurement must support that objective together. A channel can attract attention without producing the desired action. Keep product claims, dates, fees and outcomes accurate.

METHOD AND QUALITY
Compare results using consistent time periods and definitions. Test a meaningful difference rather than changing everything at once. Do not infer long-term performance from one successful post or assume a platform metric represents revenue.

COMMON MISTAKE
A learner may recognise the terminology but still be unable to demonstrate the result. Avoid replacing a practical check with a statement that the work looks correct. Keep the input, expected outcome and observed outcome so that someone else can understand your conclusion.

lessons.concept:
MEANING
Document behaviour, states and implementation-relevant decisions.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE

lessons.concept:
MEANING
Define a question before choosing a dataset or tool.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
Data questions is one part of data literacy, rather than a substitute for the whole workflow. Connect it to the course purpose when deciding what information or preparation is needed, and to data types when checking what should happen next. State which decisions belong to the user, the tool and the person reviewing the work.

PRINCIPLES
Analysis answers a defined question with data whose meaning is understood. Keep an unchanged source copy and document the field definitions. Missing values, duplicate records and inconsistent dates can change results substantially. A chart is an explanation of data, not a substitute for checking the calculation.

METHOD AND QUALITY
Use explicit denominators for rates and confirm totals independently. State the size and limits of the sample. A relationship in observed data does not by itself prove that one factor caused another.

COMMON MISTAKE
A learner may recognise the terminology but still be unable to demonstrate the result. Avoid replacing a practical check with a statement that the work looks correct. Keep the input, expected outcome and observed outcome so that someone else can understand your conclusion.

lessons.title: Collaboration agreements
lessons.intro: This lesson in Remote Collaboration develops collaboration agreements. By the end, you should be able to explain the idea, apply it to a small practical task, identify a likely mistake and justify how you checked the result. The focus is on usable foundation skills and evidence of learning.
lessons.concept:
MEANING
Define communication channels, response expectations and responsibilities.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
Collaboration agreements is one part of remote collaboration, rather than a substitute for the whole workflow. Connect it to the course purpose when deciding what information or preparation is needed, and to shared documents when checking what should happen next. State which decisions belong to the user, the tool and the person reviewing the work.

PRINCIPLES
Business technology improves a process when it reduces a measurable source of friction or helps deliver a useful outcome. Map the current workflow before choosing software. Assign ownership for records and next actions. A tool with many features can still fail if nobody follows the process.

METHOD AND QUALITY
Pilot the change with realistic sample records. Measure time, accuracy and user experience, then compare with the original process. Separate business assumptions from evidence and explain the next experiment needed to reduce uncertainty.

COMMON MISTAKE
A learner may recognise the terminology but still be unable to demonstrate the result. Avoid replacing a practical check with a statement that the work looks correct. Keep the input, expected outcome and observed outcome so that someone else can understand your conclusion.

TERMS TO CONNECT
Collaboration agreements; Shared documents; Meeting practices; Task visibility; Version management; Remote teamwork review.
steps: Explain collaboration agreements in your own words. Use the meaning above to identify its role in the course workflow.

Record the result, an identified limitation and one improvement. Keep your working notes separate from the final approved output.

project: Portfolio task for Online Research: Research a software feature using the vendor's documentation, then write a short answer with a traceable source. Document how you applied all six course concepts, include your output, record three tests and explain one improvement.

lessons.title: Research questions
lessons.intro: This lesson in Online Research develops research questions. By the end, you should be able to explain the idea, apply it to a small practical task, identify a likely mistake and justify how you checked the result. The focus is on usable foundation skills and evidence of learning.
lessons.concept:
MEANING
Define what information is needed and why.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
Research questions is one part of online research, rather than a substitute for the whole workflow. Connect it to the course purpose when deciding what information or preparation is needed, and to search techniques when checking what should happen next. State which decisions belong to the user, the tool and the person reviewing the work.

PRINCIPLES
Productivity combines useful output with an organisation system that can be maintained. Choose the tool that fits the task and define the expected result. Clear file names, consistent structure and appropriate sharing reduce avoidable confusion. Reserve time to review work rather than only producing more drafts.

METHOD AND QUALITY
Check accuracy and readability before sharing. Use version history and recoverable backups where available. A routine succeeds when it improves reliable delivery, not merely when it fills a calendar.

COMMON MISTAKE
A learner may recognise the terminology but still be unable to demonstrate the result. Avoid replacing a practical check with a statement that the work looks correct. Keep the input, expected outcome and observed outcome so that someone else can understand your conclusion.

TERMS TO CONNECT
Research questions; Search techniques; Source evaluation; Fact checking; Research notes; Research output.
steps: Explain research questions in your own words. Use the meaning above to identify its role in the course workflow.
Choose a small task connected to the course scenario below. Write the input, intended audience or user, and expected result before starting.
Apply this principle deliberately: Define what information is needed and why.
Produce a first version and check it against your expected result. Keep one ordinary test and one boundary or failure test appropriate to the task.
Record the result, an identified limitation and one improvement. Keep your working notes separate from the final approved output.
lessons.example:
COURSE SCENARIO
Research a software feature using the vendor's documentation, then write a short answer with a traceable source.

APPLICATION IN THIS LESSON
Concentrate on research questions. First identify where this idea appears in the scenario. Then explain which choice you would make and why. Use the lesson definition as the decision rule rather than choosing a tool at random.

WORKED REASONING
1. Start with the required outcome stated in the scenario.
2. Identify the input or evidence needed for research questions.
3. Apply the relevant rule: Define what information is needed and why.
4. Compare the observed output with the required outcome and record a discrepancy if one remains.
5. Improve the result and preserve a short explanation of the change.

The demonstration is complete only when its result can be inspected and its limitations are stated.
lessons.task: Complete a small demonstration of research questions within the course scenario. Submit your output or an appropriate screenshot/file, a reflection explaining your choices, two checks you performed, and one limitation or improvement. For security and account tasks, use fictional records or an authorised lab. Do not submit private passwords or real payment details.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly describes research questions?
answers: Define what information is needed and why.
It removes the need to check the final result.
It is only a decorative feature with no practical purpose.
quiz.explanation: Define what information is needed and why.

quiz.question: What should you define before applying research questions?
answers: The task, input and expected result
Only the name of the final file
A success message before doing the work
quiz.explanation: A defined outcome makes the result testable.

quiz.question: What evidence best supports a successful research questions demonstration?
answers: A visible result, a relevant check and an explanation
A claim that no review is necessary
A copied definition with no practical work
quiz.explanation: Evidence connects understanding to the actual outcome.

answers: Document the mismatch, investigate and improve the work
Hide the limitation and declare success

lessons.title: Productivity experiment
lessons.intro: This lesson in Productivity Systems develops productivity experiment. By the end, you should be able to explain the idea, apply it to a small practical task, identify a likely mistake and justify how you checked the result. The focus is on usable foundation skills and evidence of learning.
lessons.concept:
MEANING
Test one routine and evaluate output quality as well as time spent.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
Productivity experiment is one part of productivity systems, rather than a substitute for the whole workflow. Connect it to progress review when deciding what information or preparation is needed, and to the portfolio project when checking what should happen next. State which decisions belong to the user, the tool and the person reviewing the work.

PRINCIPLES
Productivity combines useful output with an organisation system that can be maintained. Choose the tool that fits the task and define the expected result. Clear file names, consistent structure and appropriate sharing reduce avoidable confusion. Reserve time to review work rather than only producing more drafts.

METHOD AND QUALITY
Check accuracy and readability before sharing. Use version history and recoverable backups where available. A routine succeeds when it improves reliable delivery, not merely when it fills a calendar.

COMMON MISTAKE
A learner may recognise the terminology but still be unable to demonstrate the result. Avoid replacing a practical check with a statement that the work looks correct. Keep the input, expected outcome and observed outcome so that someone else can understand your conclusion.

TERMS TO CONNECT
Task capture; Prioritisation; Time planning; Reusable routines; Progress review; Productivity experiment.
steps: Explain productivity experiment in your own words. Use the meaning above to identify its role in the course workflow.

Apply this principle deliberately: Test one routine and evaluate output quality as well as time spent.
Produce a first version and check it against your expected result. Keep one ordinary test and one boundary or failure test appropriate to the task.
Record the result, an identified limitation and one improvement. Keep your working notes separate from the final approved output.
